name: Heparin sodium gel

card.summary: A topical anticoagulant gel (commonly 1000 IU/g) used in Europe for bruises and superficial vein problems, and used by people hoping to fade bruising and under-eye discolouration.
card.note: Availability varies by country; broken skin and bleeding conditions are cautions on labels.

quick.overview:
Heparin sodium gel is a topical form of heparin, a naturally occurring anticoagulant, typically sold in Europe for local vein-related symptoms and bruises. Appearance-minded users apply it to bruised areas with the aim of helping discolouration clear faster.

Reviews of topical heparin cover superficial thrombophlebitis and venous insufficiency, where 1000 IU/g gel was more effective than placebo in reducing signs and symptoms. Studies specific to cosmetic bruising or depuffing are not part of those reviews.
quick.how: People apply a thin layer of the gel to the affected area as directed on the product label, often for several days. In appearance discussions it is used after minor knocks or procedures that cause bruising.
quick.risks: Topical heparin has shown good tolerability in reviews. Labels generally advise against use on open wounds and caution in people with bleeding disorders or a history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Systemic heparin carries bleeding risks, but the gel is applied locally.

lead: Heparin is a natural glycosaminoglycan anticoagulant, discovered in 1916 by Jay McLean working with William Henry Howell, and used for decades as an injected blood thinner [1]. A gel containing sodium heparin, commonly 1000 IU per gram, is used topically in many European markets for local symptoms of peripheral vascular disorders [2].

People interested in appearance use it on bruises and discolouration with the idea that it improves local microcirculation and reduces clotting in superficial tissue. A 2025 narrative review reports that topical heparin and heparinoid products improve skin microcirculation in healthy people, with effects dependent on concentration and formulation [3].
Published studies focus on superficial thrombophlebitis and venous disease rather than cosmetic outcomes [2][4][5].

chain: Bruise or discoloured area clears sooner
angle.text: Users apply the gel to bruised areas and sometimes discoloured zones to speed up the fading of visible marks. The claim rests on heparin's local circulation effects rather than on cosmetic trials.

infobox: Varies by country; widely sold in Europe

paras: Medical uses center on superficial thrombophlebitis, varicose syndromes and venous insufficiency [2][3]. In appearance contexts people use it on bruising.

A review of 20 studies with 1,055 patients found 1000 IU/g heparin gel more effective than placebo in reducing signs and symptoms of superficial thrombophlebitis, and a liposomal 2400 IU/g gel was as effective as subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin for local symptoms [4]. In head-to-head comparisons the 1000 IU/g gel was superior to a heparinoid cream in some vascular patients [4].

Heparin binds antithrombin, greatly increasing its inactivation of thrombin and factor Xa, so it prevents new clots rather than dissolving old ones [1]. Topical products are reported to provide anticoagulant and anti-inflammatory effects and to improve microcirculation and skin permeability [3].
Systemic heparin can cause bleeding and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia [1]. A 2023 review describes the 1000 IU/g gel as having an excellent tolerability profile [2].

Reviews of topical heparin cover superficial thrombophlebitis and venous insufficiency [2][4][5]. A 2025 narrative review covers topical heparin and heparinoid products for venous disorders [3]. Trials specific to cosmetic bruising or under-eye appearance were not identified in these sources.

timeline.event: Jay McLean, working with William Henry Howell, isolates an anticoagulant later named heparin [1].
